Policies

A policy is the agent's whole behaviour written down: for every state, a probability for every action. It can be a fixed arrow per cell, pure chance, or anything in between. Everything that follows in this course is about finding a good one.

Lesson 19's icy world with one change: ordinary moves now pay 0 instead of −1, so only 🏁 (+10) and 🕳️ (−10) score, and both end the episode. An action goes where it was meant 80% of the time and slips sideways 10% each way. The arrows start as Lesson 19's route. Click a cell to turn its arrow.

Each cell's four arrows are drawn with strength $\pi(a \mid s)$. This panel shows the cell you clicked last. Slide $\varepsilon$ to blend every arrow with chance.

The maths

A policy $\pi$ gives the probability of each action in each state:

$$\pi(a \mid s) = \Pr\{A_t = a \mid S_t = s\}$$

It depends only on the current state, not the time or the history. For every state the probabilities must add up to one:

$$\pi(a \mid s) \ge 0, \qquad \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s) = 1$$

So a policy is one probability distribution per state. A deterministic policy puts all the probability on one action and is often written $a = \pi(s)$. With 4 actions and 16 non-terminal cells, there are $4^{16}$ deterministic policies, and infinitely many stochastic ones.

The slider mixes your arrow with a uniformly random choice, the same idea as ε-greedy in Lesson 3:

$$\pi(a \mid s) = (1 - \varepsilon)\,\mathbb{1}[a = \text{arrow}(s)] + \frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{A}|}$$

The arrow's action gets $1 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon/4$, every other action gets $\varepsilon/4$.

A policy plus the MDP's dynamics $p(s' \mid s, a)$ gives the probability of moving between states:

$$p_\pi(s' \mid s) = \sum_{a} \pi(a \mid s)\, p(s' \mid s, a)$$

The choice of action disappears into a weighted sum. Fixing a policy turns an MDP into a Markov chain (Lesson 16): the agent still moves at random, but nothing is chosen any more.
